Suppose
sup-POZE
v.t.
From Latin supponere, to put under, to substitute, through French supposer. Webster 1828: to lay down or state as a proposition or fact that may exist; to imagine; to think. Our Lord repeatedly uses it to introduce an assumption He is about to demolish.

Biblical Definition

Suppose ye is one of Christ’s standing formulas for exposing a comfortable assumption. The hardest instance is His own account of what He came to do: Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division (Luke 12:51). The peace He gives is peace with God (Romans 5:1), and its arrival in a fallen household divides it — a fact the following verses spell out family member by family member. He uses the same construction of the Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled and the eighteen on whom the tower fell, and in both cases the answer is Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish (Luke 13:3). The word also marks honest human estimation. Peter corrects a crowd’s hasty reading of Pentecost: these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day (Acts 2:15). And John closes his Gospel with a supposition offered as reverent hyperbole: I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written (John 21:25).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SUPPOSE as to lay down or state as a proposition or fact that may exist or be true, though not known or believed to be true; to imagine; to think; to receive as true.

SUPPOSE, v.t. — To lay down or state as a proposition or fact that may exist or be true, though not known or believed to be so.

To imagine; to believe; to receive as true.

To imply; to admit as previously existing; as, the effect supposes a cause.

To think; to be of opinion; as, I suppose it to be so.

Latin supponere, from sub, under, and pono, to put — to place under as a ground of reasoning.

Key Scripture

Luke 12:51 — "Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division:"

Luke 13:3 — "I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish."

Acts 2:15 — "For these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day."

John 21:25 — "And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen."

Modern Corruption

Luke 12:51 is Christ denying in His own words the sentimental portrait of Him as a teacher of universal harmony, and it is among the most consistently avoided verses in modern preaching.

expand to see more

Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division. The verse is not a qualification of the gospel of peace but an honest statement of its effect in a world at enmity with God. Christ is the Prince of Peace and reconciles sinners to the Father; that same reconciliation sets the reconciled at odds with those who refuse it, and the following verses in Luke 12 name the fault lines as running through the household itself. The sentimental Jesus of modern religious imagination — affirming, inclusive, chiefly concerned with harmony — cannot say this sentence, which is why it is so seldom read. Where the church adopts that portrait, it loses the ability to call anything sin, since the calling would produce the division the portrait was constructed to avoid.

Luke 13:3 shows the same formula turned on a favourite instinct: the assumption that catastrophe indicates worse-than-ordinary guilt in its victims. Christ denies it flatly, and then refuses to leave the questioners comfortable — except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. Both halves must be kept. The first forbids reading providence as a scoreboard, which is the error of Job’s comforters and of every modern pronouncement that a disaster was judgment on the people who suffered it. The second forbids concluding that because the victims were no worse, the survivors are safe. Scripture’s use of catastrophe is not diagnostic of the dead but hortatory to the living.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dokeo (G1380), to think or suppose; nomizo (G3543), to hold by custom, to suppose; hupolambano (G5274), to take up, to assume; oimai (G3633), to expect or suppose.

expand to see more

Greek dokeo (G1380) — to think, to seem, to suppose; Suppose ye that I am come to give peace? (Luke 12:51).

Greek hupolambano (G5274) — to take up, and so to assume; as ye suppose (Acts 2:15).

Greek oimai (G3633) — to suppose or expect; John’s closing estimate (John 21:25).

Greek nomizo (G3543) — to suppose by custom or convention; used of mistaken assumptions throughout Acts.

Greek diamerismos (G1267) — division, dissension; what Christ says He came to bring (Luke 12:51).

Usage

"Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay (Luke 12:51) — Christ denying the sentimental portrait in His own words."

"Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish (Luke 13:3) — catastrophe is hortatory to the living, not diagnostic of the dead."

"These are not drunken, as ye suppose (Acts 2:15) — a crowd’s hasty reading corrected by the hour of the day."
